strengths: Well-motivated problem: virtual screening over ultra-large combinatorial synthesis libraries (CSLs) is a real bottleneck in drug discovery, and the 'approximate-but-exhaustive' framing—exhaustive evaluation of an approximate surrogate rather than partial evaluation of an expensive oracle—is a clean and useful conceptual contribution.

The core technical idea is sound and elegant: factorizing surrogate predictions into cached per-synthon associative contributions reduces exhaustive scoring of a 10B-compound library to a few TFLOPs, enabling top-k retrieval over tens of billions of compounds in seconds on a single T4 GPU. The errors-in-variables motivation for training the surrogate with embedding noise (Sec. 4.3) is a thoughtful statistical argument connecting surrogate training to factorization robustness.

Significant community contribution in the form of an open, fully annotated benchmark: a 10B-compound BRICS-based CSL with a 12M exhaustively docked subset (5 targets via AutoDock Vina) plus 28 RDKit physicochemical endpoints, enabling exact ground-truth top-k evaluation for arbitrary objective/constraint queries. This addresses a genuine reproducibility gap relative to proprietary libraries like Enamine REAL.

Evaluation is multi-faceted: top-j-at-k recall under six constraint sets, constraint satisfaction rates, recall-vs-budget curves comparing the factorized and non-factorized surrogate, a comparison against Thompson sampling (Klarich et al., 2024) at matched budgets, docking score enrichment on the 70B Enamine REAL library zero-shot, and detailed runtime benchmarks (GPU vs CPU, varying k and constraints).

The appendix provides valuable supporting analysis: an error decomposition (surrogate error vs. factorizer error, with a negligible cross term, Appendix A.6/Fig. 8), full architecture and training details, and the GPU top-k implementation description. Code and model weights are released.
The paper is honest about limitations in places, e.g., no synthetic feasibility guarantees, no extensive hyperparameter tuning, and degraded zero-shot performance on MET in the Enamine application.
weaknesses: Retrieval accuracy is more modest than the framing suggests. At k = 100,000 (0.8% of the 12M library), recall of the ground truth top-100 is roughly 0.75–0.8 unconstrained but drops substantially under tighter constraint sets (e.g., ~0.3–0.5 for Astex Rule of 3 and Pfizer 3/75), and for j = 100,000 it falls below ~0.2 (Fig. 2). The abstract's claim of 'consistently strong performance' and the conclusion's 'high recall rates' overstate what the figures show; many true top compounds remain missed.

Fig. 10 undercuts the central value proposition: at matched evaluation budgets, the non-factorized surrogate (which requires no library-structural assumption) achieves recall comparable to, and often slightly better than, the APEX-factorized surrogate. This indicates the factorization contributes speed and amortization rather than retrieval quality, and that APEX's accuracy is bounded by the surrogate's sample-based performance. The paper does not clearly acknowledge or discuss this near-parity.

The baseline comparison is narrow. Thompson sampling is the only external method, run unconstrained and only on the five largest reactions of the 12M library. No comparison to V-SYNTHES (the natural synthon-based baseline for docking), active learning (MolPal-style), or dense-retrieval methods (ConPLex/DrugCLIP), despite these being discussed at length in related work. This makes it hard to judge APEX's practical standing among screening approaches.

The additive synthon-contribution assumption is a strong modeling restriction for docking: protein-ligand interactions often involve coupled contributions across fragments (e.g., a hinge binder bridging two synthons), which a sum of per-(R-group, synthon) terms cannot represent. The paper quantifies the resulting factorizer error but does not analyze when or why the additive model fails, nor compare against interaction-aware factorizations (e.g., pairwise or bilinear synthon-synthon terms).

Data leakage and validity concerns: the surrogate is trained on a 1M-compound subset while evaluation uses the 12M/10B libraries built by the same BRICS fragmentation of ZINC22 molecules; synthon overlap between the labeled 1M and the evaluation libraries is not discussed, so generalization to 'new' chemical matter may be overstated. Additionally, the abstract promises a benchmark of 'more than 10 million compounds' while the fully enumerated labeled set is 12M—the 10B library itself has no ground-truth labels, so claims about the 10B/70B libraries rest on distributional enrichment (eCDFs) rather than retrieval accuracy.

Zero-shot transfer to Enamine REAL shows material degradation (MET's factorized R-squared drops sharply, and enrichment is weakest there), indicating the method is sensitive to library/reaction shift; the paper mentions this but does not probe causes or remedies.

Minor presentation issues: incomplete code URL in the footnote ('https://github.com/ Please refer to the README'), a typo in the abstract ('physicohemical'), Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse, and some claims (e.g., 'theoretical underpinnings') overstate what is a fairly straightforward linear-factorization argument.
